diseases.name: Anthracnose
diseases.plant_parts_affected: Leaves, panicles, twigs, blossoms, and fruits (distinct foliar and postharvest fruit symptoms)
diseases.description: Anthracnose is the most widespread and commercially damaging fungal disease affecting mango crops globally. While foliar symptoms manifest as necrotic leaf spots, latent fungal infections can later devastate developing blossoms and harvested mature fruits.
visible_symptoms: Small, dark-brown or black angular necrotic spots on leaves
Spots enlarge and coalesce, forming large irregular dead patches
Leaf shot-hole effect where brittle center lesions drop out
Leaf curling and premature leaf drop in severe foliar outbreaks
Blossom blight causing blackening and drop of flower clusters
Sunken black lesions with salmon-pink spore masses on fruits under humid conditions
diseases.favorable_conditions: Frequent warm rains, high relative humidity (>95%), and temperatures between 24°C and 30°C.
prevention: Prune dead twigs and open the tree canopy to enhance sun penetration and air circulation
Avoid overhead irrigation that splashes water and conidia between canopies
Maintain clean orchard sanitation by raking and destroying fallen diseased foliage and mummified fruit
Time copper-based preventative sprays to coincide with new leaf flushes and early flowering stages
management_recommendations: Sanitary pruning: cut back infected branch tips 5-10 cm into healthy wood with sterilized shears
Hot water dip treatment (48°C for 20 minutes) for harvested fruits to suppress latent postharvest anthracnose
Integrate biocontrol agents such as Bacillus subtilis or Trichoderma viride where approved locally
Consult local extension schedules for registered fungicide options (e.g., azoxystrobin or copper oxychloride)
recommended_next_steps: Inspect the entire orchard block to determine the extent of leaf blighting and blossom involvement
Isolate severely affected young saplings
Consult a certified local agricultural extension officer for regional spray calendars and pathogen confirmation
references: ICAR - Central Institute for Subtropical Horticulture (CISH) Mango Pathology Guidelines
FAO Plant Production and Protection Series: Major Mango Diseases and Postharvest Management
University of Florida IFAS Extension: Anthracnose on Mango (Publication #PP-24)
diseases.important_limitations: Visual foliar classification cannot ascertain whether latent systemic infection has colonized blossom panicles or unblemished developing fruit.

diseases.name: Bacterial Canker / Black Spot
diseases.plant_parts_affected: Leaves, petioles, tender stems, and young developing fruits
diseases.description: Bacterial canker (also known as bacterial black spot) is a severe bacterial disease causing raised, necrotic lesions with characteristic yellowish halos on leaves, twigs, and fruits, often causing premature fruit drop and twig dieback.
visible_symptoms: Water-soaked, angular black spots on leaves bounded by leaf veins
Distinct chlorotic yellow halos surrounding dark leaf spots
Cracking of thickened, raised leaf lesions with gummy exudate
Longitudinal black cankers oozing sap on petioles and young branches
Star-shaped cracked black cankers on developing fruits resulting in heavy fruit drop
diseases.favorable_conditions: Strong wind-driven rain, cyclones, stormy weather creating microscopic leaf abrasions, and temperatures around 25°C to 32°C.
prevention: Establish windbreaks around orchard borders to minimize mechanical wind abrasion and sand-blasting injuries
Use certified disease-free rootstocks and scions for grafting
Sterilize all pruning and harvesting tools in 10% sodium hypochlorite or 70% alcohol between trees
Avoid pruning operations during wet or overcast weather
management_recommendations: Immediately prune and burn severely cankered twigs during dry winter or dry season
Apply protective copper-based bactericides (e.g., copper hydroxide or copper oxychloride) mixed with agricultural lime or registered bactericides
Optimize tree nutrition: balanced potassium application strengthens cell walls against bacterial penetration
recommended_next_steps: Check adjacent trees for telltale yellow-haloed angular leaf lesions
Halt any mechanical weeding or canopy work that might wound tree bark during wet spells
Contact agricultural plant pathology services for PCR or culture confirmation if canker spreads rapidly
references: EPPO Data Sheets on Quarantine Pests: Xanthomonas citri pv. mangiferaeindicae
CABI Plantwise Knowledge Bank: Mango Bacterial Canker Technical Factsheet
Australian Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry: Mango Black Spot Management
diseases.important_limitations: Early bacterial water-soaked flecks can visually resemble mechanical hail injury; laboratory culture is required for definitive pathovar determination.

diseases.name: Cutting Weevil Damage
diseases.plant_parts_affected: Tender new leaves and emerging flush shoots
diseases.description: The mango leaf-cutting weevil is a destructive curculionid beetle pest. Female weevils lay eggs near the midrib of newly emerged tender leaves and subsequently sever the leaf blade cleanly across, causing truncated leaves.
visible_symptoms: Freshly emerged leaves cut cleanly across the blade, appearing clipped by scissors
Wilting severed leaf halves littering the ground beneath the tree canopy
Stumped remnants of cut leaves hanging on branch tips with blackened margins
Small, tiny puncture marks where females oviposited along the midrib
Stunted vegetative flushes and suppressed flush growth in nursery seedlings
diseases.favorable_conditions: Flushing cycles during post-monsoon and early spring when abundant succulent tender leaves are available.
prevention: Collect and destroy (burn or compost deeply) all fallen severed leaf blades containing weevil eggs and larvae
Light ploughing or tilling of the tree basin in winter to expose pupating larvae to predatory birds and sun desiccation
Monitor young leaf flushes closely during peak vegetative growth periods
management_recommendations: Apply neem seed kernel extract (NSKE 5%) or azadirachtin as a deterrent during initial leaf flush emergence
Encourage biological predators including entomopathogenic nematodes and weaver ants (Oecophylla smaragdina)
If infestation exceeds economic threshold in young orchards, consult local IPM recommendations for targeted sprays
recommended_next_steps: Rake and safely destroy all fallen cut leaves immediately from the orchard floor
Inspect upcoming flush buds for adult weevil feeding activity
Record flush timing to schedule preventative bio-pesticide deterrence next season
references: ICAR-CISH Technical Bulletin on Insect Pests of Mango and Their Management
Agricultural Entomological Society: Deporaus marginatus Life History and Control
Tamil Nadu Agricultural University (TNAU) Agritech Portal: Mango Leaf Weevil
diseases.important_limitations: Physical leaf damage from high winds, hail, or mechanical equipment can mimic cutting damage if severed edges become weathered.

diseases.name: Die Back / Branch Canker
diseases.plant_parts_affected: Twigs, main branches, vascular trunk tissue, and stem-end of fruits
diseases.description: Die Back is a vascular fungal wilt and decline syndrome that progresses basipetally (from branch tips downwards toward the trunk). The leaves turn brown, roll upwards, and dry out while remaining attached to dead twigs, leading to significant limb loss.
visible_symptoms: Discoloration and darkening of green twigs starting from the apex downwards
Leaves wither, turn dull brown, roll upwards, and remain tenaciously attached without falling
Gum exudation (gummosis) oozing from infected bark margins
Internal vascular browning when infected twigs are sliced open longitudinally
Progressive dieback of larger scaffold limbs, leading to partial canopy collapse
diseases.favorable_conditions: High temperatures (above 30°C), atmospheric drought, water stress, soil compaction, and prior sunscald or borer injury.
prevention: Maintain adequate irrigation during dry summer months to prevent tree stress
Protect exposed scaffold limbs from sunscald using white lime or Bordeaux paste wash
Prevent trunk borer and scale insect attacks which create infection entry courts
Avoid deep root pruning or severe root zone disturbances during cultivation
management_recommendations: Prune diseased shoots at least 10-15 cm below the discolored wood boundary into healthy tissue
Immediately seal pruning cut surfaces with Bordeaux paste, copper oxychloride paste, or grafting wax
Disinfect pruning saws between consecutive cuts
Foliar and bark drench with systemic fungicides (e.g., thiophanate-methyl or carbendazim) as per regional guidelines
recommended_next_steps: Perform sanitary pruning of all dead twigs during dry weather
Check tree trunk and scaffold limbs for gummosis and stem borer holes
Engage an arborist or agronomist if dieback extends into the main trunk
references: ICAR-Central Institute for Subtropical Horticulture: Guidelines for Mango Dieback Control
APS Plant Disease: Lasiodiplodia theobromae Associated with Stem Canker and Dieback of Mango
FAO Compendium of Tropical Fruit Crop Pathologies
diseases.important_limitations: Vascular dieback symptoms can be confounded with severe drought stress, root rot (Phytophthora), or stem-borer girdling without examining internal vascular staining.

diseases.name: Gall Midge Infestation
diseases.plant_parts_affected: Leaves, tender shoots, and young inflorescence axes
diseases.description: The mango gall midge is a cecidomyiid dipteran fly whose larvae feed within leaf tissues, stimulating abnormal gall formation. Heavy galling reduces photosynthetic surface area, induces leaf distortion, and weakens young trees.
visible_symptoms: Small, wart-like or cone-shaped raised galls (1-3 mm) on leaf blades
Galls initially appear yellowish-green, turning reddish-brown, and finally black with age
Tiny exit holes visible on the underside of old galls where adult midges emerged
Severe leaf distortion, curling, and premature drying in heavily infested flushes
Weakened vegetative flushes with reduced bloom potential in following season
diseases.favorable_conditions: High humidity, overcast weather, and synchronized vegetative flushing in spring and autumn.
prevention: Deep raking or light tilling around the drip-line to expose overwintering pupae to sunlight and natural predators
Prune lower canopy suckers and overcrowded branches to lower canopy humidity
Monitor newly emerging leaf flushes with yellow sticky traps
management_recommendations: Prune off heavily galled twigs during annual postharvest pruning and safely incinerate
Conserve natural hymenopteran parasitoids (e.g., Platygaster spp. and Tetrastichus spp.) by avoiding non-target broad-spectrum sprays
Apply targeted biorational sprays (such as neem oil 3%) when midge adults begin egg-laying on newly emerging flush
recommended_next_steps: Check underside of galled leaves for exit holes to determine if adults have already emerged
Schedule orchard floor cultivation beneath affected trees
Deploy yellow sticky cards to track adult population spikes
references: CAB International: Procontarinia matteiana (Mango Gall Midge) Distribution and Impact
Journal of Agricultural Science: Biology and Management of Cecidomyiid Pests in Mangifera indica
ICAR Technical Handbook on Fruit Crop Protection
diseases.important_limitations: Mature spent galls may persist on leaves for multiple seasons after the insect has departed; presence of galls does not always denote an active infestation.

diseases.name: Healthy Foliage
diseases.description: The specimen exhibits vibrant, normal foliar characteristics consistent with vigorous mango plant tissue. No obvious visual lesions, fungal coatings, bacterial cankers, or typical insect galls are detected in the analyzed frame.
visible_symptoms: Uniform rich green color across the lamina (or characteristic reddish-copper in tender young flushes)
Smooth leaf blade margins without tears, ragged cuts, or necrosis
Clear, unblemished leaf veins with no water-soaking or yellow halos
Absence of powdery mildew, black velvety moulds, or necrotic brown spot lesions
Firm, glossy turgid leaf texture
diseases.favorable_conditions: Balanced soil fertility, appropriate soil drainage, regular sunlight, and proper orchard canopy ventilation.
prevention: Continue routine orchard monitoring and scouting for early pest/disease incursions
Maintain balanced fertilization with compost, nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, and micronutrients (zinc, boron)
Adopt drip irrigation or basin irrigation rather than overhead sprinkling
Follow seasonal hygiene and sanitation practices
management_recommendations: No remedial or chemical intervention is needed at this time
Preserve beneficial predator insect populations in the canopy
Record seasonal flush patterns and keep periodic digital health records
recommended_next_steps: Continue standard cultural care and periodic inspections
Re-evaluate if unusual discoloration or spotting develops after rainy spells
Review seasonal preventative spray guidelines as blossom emergence nears
references: FAO Mango Good Agricultural Practices (GAP) Manual
ICAR-CISH Standard Mango Cultivation Handbook
UC Davis Fruit and Nut Research and Information Center: Mango Care
diseases.important_limitations: A healthy visual assessment reflects only the photographed leaf surface. It cannot rule out latent root pathogens (e.g., Phytophthora), sub-clinical viral diseases, or internal fruit disorders.

diseases.name: Powdery Mildew
diseases.plant_parts_affected: Inflorescence panicles, flower blossoms, tender leaves, and young developing fruitlets
diseases.description: Powdery Mildew is an obligate parasitic fungal disease of paramount economic importance during flowering. The fungus produces a superficial white or grayish powdery efflorescence over floral and foliar tissues, preventing pollination and causing catastrophic fruit drop.
visible_symptoms: White to grayish powdery coating resembling talcum powder on leaves and panicles
Powdery patches along the leaf midrib and main veins on either surface
Purplish-brown discolored lesions beneath the powdery fungal growth
Leaf distortion, curling, and brittleness in young infected leaves
Complete blighting of floral panicles, causing flowers to drop before fruit set
Premature drop of infected pea-sized fruitlets with scabby fruit skins
diseases.favorable_conditions: Cool nights (10°C to 15°C) paired with warm dry days (25°C to 30°C) and morning mists or high atmospheric humidity during flowering.
prevention: Prune dense canopy foliage to enhance air movement and reduce microclimate humidity
Eradicate infected malformed panicles and wild host plants around the orchard
Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization during pre-bloom flushes which produces overly tender, susceptible tissues
management_recommendations: Apply wettable sulfur sprays (0.2%) during early bloom emergence as a standard preventative treatment
Employ systemic triazole fungicides (such as hexaconazole, penconazole, or myclobutanil) if mildew symptoms appear on emerging blossom panicles
Rotate fungicide chemical classes with different FRAC modes of action to prevent fungal resistance development
Spray in the early morning or evening to avoid pollinator disruption and sulfur phytotoxicity under high temperatures
recommended_next_steps: Immediately inspect flower panicles across all trees for powdery fungal dust
Check regional agricultural alerts for bloom-stage powdery mildew warnings
Contact local extension advisors for weather-based fungicide spray schedules
references: APS Plant Disease: Biology and Epidemiology of Mango Powdery Mildew
ICAR-CISH Technical Bulletin: Powdery Mildew Management in Subtropical Mango Orchards
CABI Crop Protection Compendium: Oidium mangiferae datasheet
diseases.important_limitations: White residues from agricultural chemical sprays, dust, or mealybug secretions can superficially resemble powdery mildew to the untrained eye.

diseases.name: Sooty Mould
diseases.plant_parts_affected: Leaf surfaces, green twigs, and fruit peel
diseases.description: Sooty Mould is a non-parasitic superficial fungus that grows purely saprophytically on sticky honeydew excretions produced by sap-sucking insects (such as mango hoppers, scale insects, and mealybugs). It creates a dark velvety black crust that impairs photosynthesis.
visible_symptoms: Dense, continuous black velvety film or charcoal-like crust coating the upper leaf surface
The black coating can often be rubbed or peeled off, revealing intact green tissue underneath
Presence of sticky, glistening honeydew droplets on adjacent foliage and twigs
Active presence of insect vectors (leafhoppers, soft scales, whiteflies, aphids) on the canopy
Reduced tree vigor and yellowing under chronic extensive leaf coverage
Black disfigurement on fruit peel downgrading market value
diseases.favorable_conditions: Heavy infestations of honeydew-excreting insects, humid weather, and neglected shaded canopies.
prevention: Control sucking insect populations (especially Idioscopus hopper species) before honeydew accumulates
Prune inner cross-branches to allow sunlight and wind to dry out the canopy interior
Conserve insect predators like ladybird beetles, lacewings, and parasitic wasps
Avoid excessive nitrogen that triggers lush tender vegetative growth attractive to sucking pests
management_recommendations: Spray dilute starch solution (1 kg maida / starch in 50 liters water) on leaves; when it dries into flakes, the black mould peels off harmlessly
Apply horticultural mineral oils or potassium soap to soften and wash off the honeydew crust
Treat the underlying insect vectors using registered selective insecticides or neem formulation (azadirachtin)
Power-wash foliage with clean water jets on small garden trees to remove honeydew residues
recommended_next_steps: Inspect the underside of leaves and branch crotches for hoppers, scale insects, or mealybugs
Treat the insect vectors rather than spraying aggressive fungicides, as the mould is non-parasitic
Apply starch wash or horticultural soap during clear sunny weather to clear the leaf surface
references: ICAR-Central Institute for Subtropical Horticulture: Integrated Management of Mango Hoppers and Sooty Mould
University of Hawaii Cooperative Extension Service: Sooty Mold on Tropical Foliage
Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services: Sooty Molds Factsheet
diseases.important_limitations: Sooty mould is a secondary symptom of an active insect infestation; treating the mould without controlling the sap-sucking pests will result in prompt recurrence.
